newsitem.title: GERMANY: Koebnick-EU states must avoid creative accounting.
newsitem.headline: Koebnick-EU states must avoid creative accounting.

text.p: Bundesbank council member Hans-Juergen Koebnick said on Wednesday that European Union members must not resort to creative accounting to meet the entry requirements for European economic and monetary union.

Making a one-off effort to meet the fiscal criteria in 1997, the key year for deciding which countries qualify for the scheduled launch of the single currency or Euro in 1999, was not enough to guarantee the Euro's stability, Koebnick said.
"Monetary union is a long-term project, so public deficits must be reduced in the member states in a similarly long-term fashion," Koebnick said according to the text of a speech.
"That is why creative accounting is no replacement for genuine consolidation."
The speech was released ahead of delivery to a conference in Trier. Koebnick is also president of the state central bank for Rhineland-Palatinate and Saarland.
Koebnick said it was decisive for the stability of the Euro that the criteria laid down in the Maastricht Treaty were strictly maintained.

But he added that the Treaty allowed some divergence from the reference levels which state that a country's budget deficit must not exceed three percent of GDP, and its public debt must be no higher than 60 percent.
"The Treaty does not demand a deficit ratio of exactly three percent," Koebnick said.

"It allows a value above this reference level, provided that the deficit ratio has permanently fallen in the years before, or that it only exceeds the three percent level exceptionally or temporarily, and that the deficit ratio remains near the reference value."
The 60 percent level could also be exceeded provided it was falling and rapidly approaching the reference level, Koebnick said.

He also said it was conceivable that almost all EU members unable to sign up for monetary union in 1999 could join by 2002, when Euro notes and coin will be issued and the three-year transition to full monetary union ends.

"By the time the introduction of a new currency becomes visible and tangible in the form of notes and coin in this new currency, that means by January 1, 2002, these states have three years to achieve the necessary convergence."

"This period should be sufficient for most of the EU states. This means that by January 1, 2002 all states in the European Union -- with one exception perhaps -- could be members of European monetary union."
